questions.prompt: Dopamine is best described as the chemical of…
questions.explanation: Dopamine drives the 'wanting' more than the 'liking' — which is why urges can outlast any real enjoyment.

questions.prompt: When you ride out an urge without acting, over time your brain…
options: Gets permanently more sensitive to the cue
Learns the cue no longer predicts the reward
questions.explanation: This is called extinction: each un-acted-on urge weakens the link between cue and reward.

questions.prompt: A flat, low-motivation stretch early in recovery usually means…
options: The brain is recalibrating its baseline
questions.explanation: The 'flatline' is the reward system resetting. It tends to pass as ordinary rewards start to feel good again.

options: Keeps rising until you give in
Rises, peaks, and falls within minutes
questions.explanation: Urges follow a wave. If you don't feed or fight them, they crest and fall — usually within minutes.

options: Observing the urge without acting on it
Giving in quickly to get it over with
questions.explanation: You notice and allow the wave without obeying it — neither suppressing nor acting.

questions.prompt: The most helpful response to a single slip is…
options: Decide you've failed and stop trying
Get curious about what triggered it
questions.explanation: Curiosity beats shame. A slip is data about the loop, and self-criticism feeds the very stress that drives it.
